1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn back at once with the queen, and accepts that White gains a tempo by attacking the queen with Nc3. In return Black gets a free game: easy development and a sound pawn structure, with no weakness to defend.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.background: The more “tactical” of the two main branches of the Scandinavian Defence, known as the Modern Scandinavian. John Emms calls 3.d4 White's main line against it.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Delays the recapture so that the queen does not lose a tempo, and wins the pawn back with the knight later. White may try to keep the pawn, but usually just develops; the game turns more tactical, with Black aiming for quick development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nd7.strategy: Aims at ...Ngf6 and ...Nb6 to win back d5, but blocks both the c8-bishop and the queen's pressure on the pawn. White can hold it easily and stays a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Na6.strategy: Heads for b4 to pressure d5 and c2, but the knight starts on the rim, and White holds the pawn with c4 or Nc3 and stays a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's own pressure on d5 and does nothing to win the pawn back. White keeps it with c4 or Nc3, and the bishop on d7 is passive.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop but does nothing against d5, and White holds the pawn with c4 or Nc3 and stays a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qd7.strategy: Attacks d5 along the file but blocks the c8-bishop. White defends with c4 or Nc3 and keeps the extra pawn while the queen has done nothing useful.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qd6.strategy: Attacks d5, but after 3.Nc3 White keeps the pawn, and the exposed queen can be hit with tempo, for instance by Nb5.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nh6.strategy: Aims for ...Nf5, but the knight on the rim does nothing for d5. White holds the pawn easily, and Black is a pawn down with a misplaced piece.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 a6.strategy: Wastes a move on a flank pawn and leaves d5 where it stands. White keeps the pawn with c4 or Nc3 and has lost nothing in development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 a5.strategy: Advances the a-pawn for no purpose: nothing is developed, d5 is not recaptured, and the move only weakens b5.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which would hit d5 along the long diagonal, but White holds the pawn easily and stays a pawn up with the better development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Blackburne–Kloosterboer Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6.background: Joseph Blackburne played it successfully on at least one occasion, but after 3.dxc6 it is thought to be unsound and is almost never seen in master-level play.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6.strategy: Offers a pawn for development: after 3.dxc6 Nxc6 Black's pieces come out quickly on open lines, but White stays a clean pawn up and can finish development in peace.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c5.strategy: Offers the c-pawn: after 3.dxc6 en passant Nxc6 the position is the same as in the 2...c6 gambit, a pawn down for some development. White can also simply keep the d5 pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e6.strategy: Offers the e-pawn: after 3.dxe6 Bxe6 Black has only the bishop out for it, and White stays a pawn up and develops freely.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5.strategy: Grabs central space and opens the f8-bishop, but does not recapture on d5. After 3.Nc3 White holds the pawn with a developing move, and Nf3 then pressures the unsupported e5 pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 g6.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto, but the d5 pawn stays with White, who holds it easily and is simply a pawn up.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 h6.strategy: A waiting move on the rim: nothing is developed, d5 is not recaptured, and White holds the pawn with c4 or Nc3.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 h5.strategy: A wing advance that neither develops a piece nor recaptures. It weakens g5 and leaves White a clean extra pawn after c4 or Nc3.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nc6.strategy: Loses a piece: the d5 pawn attacks c6, so 3.dxc6 takes the knight, and ...bxc6 recovers only a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Be6.strategy: Loses a piece: 3.dxe6 takes the bishop, and ...fxe6 recovers only a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bg4.strategy: Loses the bishop: nothing defends g4, and with the e-pawn gone from the diagonal the queen takes it at once with Qxg4.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Bh3.strategy: Loses the bishop for nothing: gxh3 or Nxh3 takes it, and no piece of Black's defends h3.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the queen's own pressure on d5, and 3.Bb5+ already checks the king on the open diagonal. The pawn stays with White.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 b5.strategy: Hangs a second pawn: 3.Bxb5+ wins it with check, and the d5 pawn is still White's.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 f6.strategy: Leaves the d5 pawn and takes the f6 square from the g8-knight. It weakens e6 and opens the e8-h5 diagonal for 3.Qh5+, damaging the king's cover for nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 f5.strategy: Opens the e8-h5 diagonal: 3.Qh5+ is check at once and forces Black to weaken g6 or move the king, while the d5 pawn stays with White.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 g5.strategy: Loosens f6 and h6 and makes the g5 pawn a target for the c1-bishop once d4 opens its diagonal, while the d5 pawn stays with White.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.dxc6.strategy: Takes the second pawn offered. White is now two pawns up, and the gambit is unsound: Black has only some development to show for the material, which White can answer by calmly completing its own.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.d4.strategy: Builds the centre at once and gives the pawn back: after ...cxd5 the pawn structure is symmetrical and solid and the material is level. It is a sound way to meet the gambit, but it throws away the extra pawn the gambit offers.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and defends d5, but cannot hold the pawn against the attack of the c-pawn and the queen: Black recaptures with ...cxd5 and the material is level again. White gets a natural development, but gives up the extra pawn for it.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.dxc6 Nxc6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Blackburne Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.dxc6 Nxc6.strategy: The natural recapture and the principal answer: the knight develops towards the centre and the c8-bishop is freed, so Black pays a pawn for a lead in development. Without a d-pawn Black has to make that lead count quickly, and White can answer by calmly completing its own development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.dxc6 e5.name: Scandinavian Defence: Kloosterboer Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.dxc6 e5.strategy: Gives up a second pawn for open lines for the king's bishop and the queen, with no concrete threat to show for it. White is two pawns ahead, and the advanced pawn on c6 cramps Black by attacking b7 and d7, so White simply develops.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 c6 3.dxc6 bxc6.strategy: Recaptures with the b-pawn, which leaves Black with isolated a- and c-pawns and no d-pawn, and without the quick development of the knight recapture. Black is simply a pawn down with a worse structure and nothing to show for it.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5 3.dxe6.strategy: Takes the offered pawn en passant, which puts White two pawns up until Black recaptures on e6. The gambit gives Black no more than development in return, so White has no reason to refuse and can calmly finish developing.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5 3.d4.strategy: Gives the extra pawn back at once: with the pawn on d4 in front of the queen, d5 loses its guard and ...Qxd5 regains it, and after dxe5 the queen recaptures with check. Black gets an active queen and an equal game, and White has wasted the gambit.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and defends the pawn on d5, so White keeps the extra pawn without any commitment. It is sound but modest: Black keeps the pawn on e5 and the open lines of the gambit, and White has not taken the two pawns that taking en passant wins at once.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5 3.dxe6 Bxe6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Boehnke Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5 3.dxe6 Bxe6.strategy: The natural recapture: the bishop at once becomes active on its open diagonal, so Black is only one pawn down and can develop freely. White keeps a healthy extra pawn, and Black has to pay for it with activity, but no other recapture does it as well.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5 3.dxe6 fxe6.strategy: Recaptures with the f-pawn and opens the f-file, but the king is left exposed and the c8-bishop is shut in behind its own pawn. The check on h5 gains White a tempo at once, forcing ...g6 or a king move.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 e5 3.dxe6 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece but leaves the pawn on e6 alone: White takes on f7 with check and is at least two pawns up, while Black's king is dragged into the open.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4.strategy: The main line. White gives up the idea of keeping the pawn and takes central space instead, opening lines for the queen and the c1-bishop. Black wins the pawn back, so the game turns on whether White's bigger centre outweighs Black's quick, comfortable development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4.strategy: Defends the d5 pawn with a pawn and tries to keep the extra material instead of handing it back. The cost is that the c4 pawn blocks the f1-bishop's diagonal and gives Black a target: the pawn chain can be chipped away at once, and White often has to return the pawn anyway.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.Bb5+.strategy: Checks first, so Black must put a piece or pawn in the way before taking back on d5, and White then defends the pawn. The cost is time: the bishop is exposed on b5 and may have to move again while Black develops. A respectable way to try to keep the extra pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and leaves the pawn to its fate: if the knights are traded on d5, the queen recaptures in the centre without losing a tempo. White has handed the pawn back for a quiet, equal game, which makes this harmless rather than a try for an edge.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 c6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Panov Transfer
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 c6.strategy: The most common reply: the c-pawn attacks d5 from the side and aims to open the centre. If White grabs on c6, Black recaptures with a knight and has a lead in development for the pawn, so White normally returns the pawn with a central strike, which gives an equal game.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Icelandic-Palme Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.background: Invented by Icelandic masters who looked for an alternative to the more common 3...c6.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 e6.strategy: A gambit for speed: if White takes on e6, Black's bishop recaptures with development and hits the c4 pawn. Black hopes that an open position and a lead in development outweigh the pawn, but against calm play it is simply a pawn down.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.c4 Nxd5.strategy: Takes back the pawn at once but loses a piece: after cxd5 Qxd5 Nc3 the queen has to move, and Black ends up a knight down for a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5.name: Scandinavian Defence: Marshall Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5.strategy: The natural reply: Black wins the pawn back at once with a knight that is already developed, so no time is lost. The knight stands in the centre but can be driven off by c4 while White builds a bigger centre, so Black has to avoid ending up cramped.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4.background: The line had some popularity in the late 1990s. According to a monograph by Roush, Lance and Cornell, John Donaldson christened it in 1996, recognising several Portuguese players; David Smerdon calls the name a little unfair to earlier exponents such as the Belgian IM Michel Jadoul.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4.strategy: Develops with an attack on the queen and does not hurry to recapture. White can keep the extra pawn, so this is a real gambit: Black bets on quick development and active pieces, and the game is sharp from the start.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6.strategy: A less direct way to regain the pawn: the c-pawn attacks d5 a third time and keeps Black's set-up compact, but it spends a move on a pawn instead of developing a piece. Sound, but Black is a step behind in development compared with the main reply.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Richter Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6.background: A rare move that IM Kurt Richter played on occasion in the 1930s.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto but leaves d5 alone, so White defends the pawn with c4 and keeps it, with a broad centre as well. Black has no quick way to win the pawn back and spends the next moves on a slow plan a pawn down.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3.strategy: The main move: it parries the threat to the queen and attacks the bishop at once. The cost is that f3 takes the natural square from the g1-knight and loosens the king's side, so White must castle before the centre opens, since Black is ahead in development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Nf3.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Classical Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Nf3.strategy: Meets the threat by developing a piece and does not weaken the kingside, bringing White closer to castling. The bishop pins the knight to the queen for now, but the pin is easily undone once the f1-bishop develops; the price is that the d5 pawn is offered back.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+.strategy: A check inserted before the queen is saved: Black must answer it, and the d5 pawn, which controls c6, makes one of the natural blocks risky. The threat to the queen stays, so White still has to deal with it afterwards, having used the tempo to shape how Black blocks.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Be2.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Wuss Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Be2.strategy: Sidesteps the threat by offering a bishop trade. After it Black recovers the d5 pawn with the queen, so White gives the pawn back for a quiet, safe position; it is harmless, since it asks nothing of Black's active development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ Nbd7.strategy: The usual block: the b8-knight develops and the pawn structure stays untouched. The knight is pinned to the king for now, so Black may chase the bishop away later. The threat to the queen has not gone away, so White still has to find an answer.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ c6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Elbow Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ c6.strategy: Blocks the check with the pawn and offers it. Taking the queen at once is a mistake: after dxc6 Bxd1? the discovered check c7+ wins material back with interest. Recapturing with the knight instead gives Black development for a pawn at best.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ Bd7.strategy: Blocks the check with the bishop and so gives up the attack on the queen. White retreats the bishop to e2 and keeps the d5 pawn, while Black has spent its most active piece for nothing: the lead in development, the point of the gambit, is gone.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ Nbd7.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Lusophobe Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.Bb5+ Nbd7.strategy: Meets the threat to the queen with a retreat, but the check has achieved little: Black has put the b8-knight on d7 in the process and can trade bishops and take back the pawn. White has spent two moves with the bishop, so this is a harmless line rather than a try for an edge.

Drives the bishop away with a tempo and so keeps the extra pawn. The price is a loosened king's side and an open diagonal towards the king, so White has to finish development quickly while Black's lead is still fresh. The most principled answer to the threat.

Blocks the attack on the queen with a developing move but gives the d5 pawn back: Black takes it with the knight, and the knight on f3 stays pinned to the queen. Black has an equal game and easy development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5.strategy: Keeps the bishop on its active diagonal, but g4 drives it away again and prepares g5 against the knight, so White gains space and time and keeps the pawn. Black is left cramped, and the development lead does not make up for it.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bh5.strategy: Steps back to h5, where g4 drives the bishop on to g6 with a gain of space. White keeps the extra pawn while the bishop is hunted around the board and Black develops nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bd7.strategy: Steps out of the attack and keeps the bishop flexible. The pawn on f3 has weakened White's king's side and taken the natural square from the g1-knight, so Black can win the d5 pawn back with ...c6 and use the lead in development against an uncastled king.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.g.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Correspondence Refutation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.g.strategy: The sharpest answer: the pawn hits the bishop again and prepares g5 against the f6-knight, gaining space and time while White keeps the pawn. Black's lead in development is hard to use because the knight is pushed to a passive square; the price is a loosened kingside.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.c.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Banker Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.c.background: In David Smerdon's telling, GM Zili Wang played it against Rui Damaso in a Portugal-China match in Macao in 1996 and was checkmated in thirteen moves.
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.c.strategy: Defends the pawn with a pawn, but allows ...e6: the centre opens while White is still uncastled and Black's lead in development counts for a lot, so the extra pawn is no safe asset. The sharper g4 would have kept Black cramped.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.strategy: Checks first, but Black simply develops with ...Nbd7, and the bishop on b5 can be attacked by ...a6. White wastes the moment: Black can win the d5 pawn back, whereas g4 at once would gain space and time against the bishop.

The usual block: it develops the b8-knight and keeps the c-pawn free. The knight is pinned to the king for now, so Black needs to chase the bishop away to free it, while White's task is to secure the d5 pawn before Black's lead in development tells.

Blocks the check with a pawn that attacks both the bishop and d5, offering a second pawn for open lines. After dxc6 Nxc6 the knight is pinned but well placed, and Black leads in development, though White is still a pawn up.

Interposes the bishop and offers a trade. After Bxd7+ the pin is gone and d5 is still attacked, but Black has swapped off its most active piece and White stays a pawn up. Sound, yet it surrenders the lead in development that the gambit is played for.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Jadoul Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.strategy: Secures the d5 pawn with a pawn, so Black cannot win it back easily while the knight on d7 is pinned. White holds the extra pawn and a space advantage, but the position is loose around the king, and Black plays for a central pawn break to open the game.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.name: Scandinavian Defence: Portuguese Gambit, Melbourne Shuffle Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Bg4 4.f3 Bf5 5.B.strategy: Defends d5 with a piece and develops, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so no pawn supports d5. It holds the pawn less firmly than a pawn would and gives Black targets for piece play, while White keeps the extra pawn.

Attacks the bishop with the g-pawn, so it has to retreat (capturing on g4 only loses material), and White gains space. The king's side is loosened further, so White must trust that the extra pawn and the pin on d7 outweigh the exposed king.
Takes the pinned knight with the bishop, giving up the pin that tied Black's pieces. White stays a pawn up, but Black recaptures with a developed queen and keeps the lead in development.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6.strategy: Takes a second pawn. After the recapture on c6 Black has quick development and pressure on d4, but White's centre holds and White keeps the extra pawn, so Black must play for activity. White needs care with the king in the centre.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.c4.strategy: Defends the d5 pawn and builds a broad centre, but gives the extra pawn back: once the pawns are exchanged on d5 and Black retakes, material is level. Sound and solid, though it passes up the chance to keep a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and guards d4 first, leaving the pawn structure for later. Once Black takes on d5 the material is level and the game is balanced. Flexible and sound, but it gives back the chance to keep a pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 e5.name: Scandinavian Defence: Kádas Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 e5.strategy: Offers a second pawn for nothing: White takes on b7, Black's bishop recaptures, and White is two pawns up. Black's open lines and the attack on d4 do not make up for it.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6.strategy: Recaptures with a developing move that hits d4. Black is a pawn down, but the knight comes out with tempo and the pieces get a grip on the centre, so White has to defend d4 and finish development carefully. White keeps the extra pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 bxc6.strategy: Recaptures with the b-pawn, which opens the b-file but leaves the a-pawn isolated, and develops nothing. White is a pawn up with the bigger centre and can complete development calmly. Playable but slow.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4.strategy: The natural reply: the c-pawn defends d5 and takes space, so White keeps the extra pawn, which the fianchetto cannot regain quickly. White builds a broad pawn centre, and Black has to undermine it with pieces and pawn breaks.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and guards d4, accepting that Black takes back on d5. White drives the knight away with c4 and gets more space, but the extra pawn is gone. Sound and flexible, yet a step behind defending the pawn at once.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops and covers d5, but Black just takes on d5 and the pawn is gone. The knight on c3 also blocks the c-pawn, which would have kept the pawn and built a bigger centre, so White gets a level game for nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4 b5.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation, Wing Gambit
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4 b5.strategy: A second pawn sacrificed: the b-pawn attacks the c4 pawn that guards d5, hoping to win d5 back with a gain of time. After cxb5 Black regains that pawn, but is still a pawn down with only pressure on the long diagonal as compensation.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4 Bg7.strategy: Develops the fianchetto bishop and prepares castling. Black accepts being a pawn down for lasting pressure on White's pawn centre: the bishop eyes d4 once the f6-knight steps aside, and pieces and pawn breaks can undermine it, so the game is a slow fight.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 g6 4.c4 c6.strategy: Strikes at the pawn chain at once: the c-pawn attacks d5 from the side to win the pawn back. If White grabs on c6, Black recaptures with the knight and develops with tempo, so White normally has to return the pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4.strategy: Drives the knight away with a gain of time and builds a broad centre. Black must retreat the knight and fight for a share of it; White gets a space advantage, at the price of a slightly shut-in f1-bishop and a c4 pawn that becomes a target.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and defends d4, choosing piece development over chasing the knight at once. The pawn push to c4 can follow, but meanwhile Black has time to develop the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nc3.strategy: Attacks the knight with a developing move, but Black can trade it off, and White recaptures with the b-pawn, which doubles the c-pawns. White keeps a broad pawn centre, but its structure is damaged. Playable, less ambitious than driving the knight away with the c-pawn.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nb4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Kiel Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nb4.background: Rarely seen in practice because it is difficult to play effectively; Harman and Taulbut call it "a speculative try".
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nb4.strategy: A speculative try: the knight hits c2 and d3, hoping for Qa4+ N8c6 d5? b5! with a good game. But White simply drives it back with a3, gaining time and space, so Black has spent two moves with the same knight for nothing.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nb6.strategy: Retreats to the most active square: the knight hits the c4 pawn and keeps an eye on the centre. Black accepts that White has more space and counters by undermining the pawn centre with pieces and pawn breaks. A flexible set-up with no weaknesses.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.c4 Nf6.strategy: The simple retreat: the knight goes home, covers d5 and e4, and keeps the structure intact. Black has lost time with the knight, so White's space gives a slight edge, but the position stays solid and free of weaknesses.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 Bg4.name: Scandinavian Defence: Modern Variation, Gipslis Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: The main reply: the bishop develops before ...e6 shuts it in and pins the knight to the queen, so a trade on f3 would cost White a defender of the centre. Black catches up in development at once, while White has the space and must complete development carefully.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6.name: Scandinavian Defence: Richter Variation
1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto aimed at d4. White gains time with c4 against the knight on d5 and builds a big centre, but Black's bishop will press on it for the long term. A sound alternative, though White's space is easy to play with.

1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Nf6 3.d4 Nxd5 4.Nf3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in, and prepares to trade it for White's light-squared bishop. Black aims for an even game by simple development and has no weaknesses, while White keeps a slight edge in space.
